First-instar nymphs of Chortoicetes terminifera emerge from the egg pod with a body length of 0.5 centimeters [Lb = 0.5 centimeters], a diminutive size that marks the beginning of a rapid developmental trajectory. At this initial stage, the dry weight at birth is 0.0009 grams , reflecting the limited endogenous reserves carried over from the yolk-dependent embryo. The incubation period leading to this hatchling stage, measured at a constant temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], lasts approximately 17.4 days [ab = approximately 17.4 days], a thermal regime that accelerates embryogenesis compared to the cooler conditions typical of winter diapause. The newly emerged insect, having absorbed the remaining yolk, then makes the trophic switch to active feeding commencement on host grasses, initiating the larval feeding stage that will carry it through successive instars.

As nymphs progress through the larval-juvenile phase, a pronounced increase in dry mass becomes evident at the beginning of each instar. Individuals feeding on button grass under controlled conditions record a dry weight at the beginning of instar 2 of 0.00288 grams , which more than doubles to 0.00556 grams  at the start of the third instar. This accelerating growth continues, with the dry weight at the beginning of instar 4 reaching 0.01171 grams , followed by a substantial jump to 0.0383 grams  at the onset of the fifth instar, a value that represents the product of the standard mass and a diet-linked multiplier. These sequential mass gains are fuelled by the ingestion of grasses and reflect the high food intake rate typical of orthopteran larvae during the pre-pubertal accelerating stage.

Sexual maturation in C. terminifera is attained after a well-defined duration of post-embryonic development. Under a regime maintained at 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], puberty occurs at 34.35 days since birth [tp = 34.35 days since birth], a period that encompasses the full sequence of nymphal instars leading to imaginal ecdysis. At the point of puberty, individuals achieve a dry weight of 0.1095 grams , representing the culmination of somatic growth and the onset of gametogenesis. This value is notably higher than the egg dry weight of roughly 0.0012 grams reported for this species, illustrating the nearly hundredfold increase in biomass that occurs during the larval-juvenile stage. The final somatic size of the adult is expressed by the ultimate total length of the sixth instar, which measures 3.2 centimeters [Lp = 3.2 centimeters], a dimension that defines the maximum body length before the onset of reproductive activity.

Reproductive output in this locust species is strongly modulated by temperature, with peak performance recorded under warm conditions. At a sustained ambient temperature of 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C], females exhibit a maximum reproductive rate that is best understood through two key components: each female can deposit up to 72 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = up to 72 eggs per clutch], and these oviposition events occur with a frequency of 3 clutches per 60-day adult lifespan [F_R_i = 3 clutches per 60-day adult lifespan]. This high fecundity per event is consistent with the large number of ovarioles present in the ovary and underscores the species capacity for rapid population build-up. The lifespan of the reproductively active adult under these same thermal conditions (35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C]) is approximately 94 days [am = approximately 94 days], representing the sum of the 60-day adult stage and the 34-day pre-reproductive period.

The life-history strategy of Chortoicetes terminifera is characterized by a maturation schedule that prioritizes rapid growth to a pubertal size, followed by intensive, short-lived reproduction. The transition from fertilised ovum to imago at 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C] is completed in roughly 51.75 days, a relatively compressed timeline for an acridid of this ultimate body length. Field records suggest that the population dynamics of this species are tightly linked to episodic rainfall events that create suitable oviposition substrates and promote the flush growth of host grasses. Males, which are typically smaller and more agile than females, engage in territorial patrols to secure mating opportunities with gravid individuals. The species ability to enter a facultative egg diapause during dry periods allows the population to persist through unfavorable seasons, ensuring the continuity of generations when conditions again become favorable for rapid development and high reproductive output.
